extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy; general educated readers and scholars interested in critiques of utilitarianism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and analyzes the criteria by which utilitarian and intuitive (non-utilitarian) moral theories judge actions (e.g., utility, habit-formation, conscience, truth, sanctions). Focus is on the standards used to evaluate what is 'virtue' or 'vice' and the objections to utilitarian standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilitarian principle (virtue = utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtue is only virtuous because it is useful; actions are judged by their tendency to promote or diminish happiness — 'the utilitarian rule of judging actions and dispositions by their tendency to promote or diminish happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This implies that if an act produces a net increase in happiness it is virtuous, even if outwardly considered vice. Lecky gives the extreme example: if a crime produces great immediate utility and can be kept absolutely secret so as to prevent influence on general morals, the utilitarian would be justified in performing it. The passage stresses reliance on consequences (including hidden consequences) as the sole moral standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of probability of detection and influence on public morals
rubrics_metrics.description: The morality of many acts must depend upon the probability of their detection and the likelihood that the act will become an example influencing general standards of morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky notes that utilitarian calculations must factor in whether an act will be known and thereby change social norms; this is used to explain why secrecy can affect the moral calculus, and why 'a little adroit hypocrisy' might convert vice into virtue under strict utilitarianism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit-formation / predisposition of the agent
rubrics_metrics.description: An act may be judged by whether it impairs or alters the agent's disposition, thereby predisposing him to future acts generally hurtful to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the principal attempt to evade the utilitarian conclusion that isolated beneficial acts (even crimes) might be justified. Lecky critiques it by arguing a single act rarely alters disposition enough to outweigh immediate great good, and that the habit formed might instead be precise utility-calculation — 'the habit of in all cases regulating actions by a precise and minute calculation of their utility.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote consequences and weakening of moral sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral appraisal must consider remote or long-term consequences, such as a single wrongful act weakening the sanctity of life or social respect for norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky discusses examples (e.g., exposure/murder of children among ancient Greeks, religious unveracity coexisting with business veracity) to show that some harms are localized while others might be general. He questions whether utilitarian calculations can reliably capture these diffuse, long-term effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of benevolence: duties to animals vs humans (net-happiness criterion irrespective of species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some utilitarians extend the utility calculus to animals: acts are virtuous when they produce a net result of happiness and vicious when they produce net suffering 'altogether irrespective of the question whether this enjoyment or suffering is of men or animals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky questions how, on inductive grounds, benevolence originally founded in human social interest could be extended to animals to the same extent, and points to practical and repugnant implications (e.g., comparing eating children and sheep under the same calculus). He also notes that such extension depends on associative psychology and habit-formation rather than a clear rational basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic value of truth and pursuit of truth as a moral duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth should be deemed an end distinct from and superior to utility; it is a moral duty to pursue it even if it leads to pain rather than pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky argues that utilitarianism, which values beliefs only for their utility, cannot justify the critical review of opinions when that review diminishes happiness. He uses examples of superstition providing comfort and the painful effects of losing consoling beliefs to show why truth may be pursued for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious sanction (appeal to divine will and future retribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of religious sanction treats the arbitrary will of the Deity, and the anticipation of future rewards and punishments, as the motives for virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky critiques this on several grounds: it renders the goodness of God tautological if God's will defines goodness; belief in retribution depends on a moral sense of desert; and one cannot prove a Creator's supreme goodness from induction without presupposing a moral faculty. He treats religious sanction as a distinct motive used by some utilitarians/theologians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscience as moral faculty (distinct from pleasure/pain associations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscience points out a difference between right and wrong and inflicts pain when commands are violated; it is not merely an association producing pleasure/pain but a source of legitimate moral obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky distinguishes two functions of conscience (cognitive distinction and affective sanction) and argues intuitive moralists see conscience as more than associative habit. He warns utilitarians reduce conscience to habit/association and thereby cannot account for the distinct sense of obligation ('ought'). He also notes variability: conscience causes intense pain for some and negligible for others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidence of virtue and interest (virtue as enlightened self-interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that duty strictly coincides with interest when rightly understood — a prudent person will necessarily be virtuous because moral conduct promotes one's happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky acknowledges some truth but limits its scope: it fails for nations, imperfectly organized societies, and for high forms of virtue that demand sacrifice. He argues that many virtues (heroism, intense intellectual or moral excellence) may reduce, rather than promote, personal happiness and thus are not justified by this criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and the happiness-maximising virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: If happiness is supreme, the virtues that promote happiness are those realizable with little suffering and sustained without much effort — i.e., moderation rather than extremes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky observes that very high excellence often produces suffering (e.g., genius leading to 'much grief'), and social penalties may even strike highest virtues. Thus utilitarianism tends to favor moderate virtues and is unfavourable to self-denial and heroism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of fiction, imagination, and sympathy by utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Under utilitarianism, indulgence of vicious imagination without leading to action (and without remorse) can be a net pleasure and thus applauded; likewise fiction's exercise of sympathy might 'indispose men to practical benevolence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky notes utilitarians may treat imaginative pleasures as gains if they do not produce harmful actions, but he raises the objection that frequent sympathy for imagined beings may reduce practical benevolence — a cost to be weighed in the utility calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of induction for moral knowledge and need for a moral faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction alone cannot demonstrate some things are in their own nature good or evil; knowledge of supreme excellence and moral truths derives from our moral nature (instinctive or faculty) rather than pure reason or induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lecky contends that to infer an all-perfect Creator or to ground moral absolutes from nature is impossible by induction; instead the sense of moral obligation (a moral faculty) is the primary evidence and foundation of religion and ethics. This serves as an objection to purely inductive/utilitarian foundations of morality.
